title: King and pawn vs king: the rules
author: John Bartholomew

source.title: Chess Endgame Fundamentals: King + Pawn vs. King

description: Why the slow pawn march only draws, and how taking the opposition with Kd3 wins king and pawn against king.
permissionNote: Lesson for a day of the King and Pawn Endgames course; the course permission (pending) governs it.

chapterData.name: How the slow march draws

children.comment: The consistent Kd6 is stalemate: every square around the black king is covered by the white king and pawn.
Or White moves the king away, say Kb7, and the pawn on d7 falls.
Kd8. White's choices are all bad now.
White plays d7 check, as he's done the whole game.
King c8, facing the white king. This is where most players who don't know the ending stop and think.

moves.comment: The pawn inches up again, d6 with check. Where does the black king go?

chapterData.intro: This is the march John sees all the time: White pushes the pawn up to d5 with the king behind it, and Black keeps stepping back in front of it. You're Black. Show why it's only a draw.

chapterData.name: Take the opposition: Kd3

children.comment: Black gave up c5, so the king takes it.
Also keeps the win by the engine, but it doesn't gain any ground. Which square did Black just give up?

King d4. The opposition again, so Black has to give up space.
A massive mistake: Black plays ...Ke6 and takes the opposition himself. Keep the pawn back.
Black naturally steps in front of the pawn with ...Kd6.
Outflanking: take e4, the square Black just gave up.

White is fighting for c4, d4 and e4. Black has to move and must give up at least one. Say ...Kc5, a reasonable sidestep that gives up e4.

moves.comment: King d3. Kings on the same file, on the same colour squares, an odd number of squares between them (one), and Black to move: White has the opposition.
After d3 the position is already drawn. Black holds as long as he plays correctly. Clear the squares in front of the pawn with the king first, and push only when it's safe.

chapterData.intro: You're White. The pawn queens on d8, a long way off. White to move: the march you just saw started with d3. What's the winning move?

chapterData.name: Clear the way, then push

children.comment: The opposition move, Kd6. Black would love to pass, but he has to give way, and White's king goes to the other side.
It looks right, and John admits he played it before he knew the opposition. But ...Ke8 takes the opposition: d7+ Kd8, and White must stalemate with Kd6 or give up the pawn.
...Kd8. What should White do? Pause and work it out.

moves.comment: Time to move the pawn. It hasn't left d2, so it can go two squares, and Black can't come to d5 or c5.

chapterData.intro: White repeated the process, taking the opposition and outflanking, until the kings stood on opposite sides of the pawn: White on e6, Black on c6. White has cleared the space in front of the pawn.
